answers.question: I missed Thursday and cut the long run short. Should I make up the miles next week?
answers.answer: No, do not make up the missed miles. The limiter last week was heat, sleep and stress, not fitness, and piling extra miles on a tired body is how small problems become big ones. Get back on the normal pattern this week, and if the AC is fixed and you sleep better, the long run will feel much more like itself.

new.analysis:
You made two good decisions under bad conditions. Stopping the threshold after two reps when heart rate was 174 at 8:18/mi pace, and ending the long run at 11 mi when drift hit +10 bpm, both protected the bigger picture. Over 8 weeks that judgement will matter more than any single workout.

The numbers tell the story of the week, not a fitness drop. Easy heart rate on Tuesday was 153 at 10:24/mi, versus 138 at 9:51/mi three weeks ago. That is a 13 bpm shift at a slower pace, and it tracks the heat, the 5.5 hr sleep average and the work deadline, not your legs.

The plan next week keeps the same shape, with a short marathon-pace piece on Wednesday to start pointing the work at race day. Target pace for a 3:45 finish is about 8:35/mi, and 4 miles is a conservative first dose while you are still rebuilding sleep. The long run goes back to 13 mi at easy effort, with heart rate under 150 as the ceiling; if it is above that early, slow down rather than push on.

Two housekeeping things. Please run Wednesday early, before the heat, and carry water on anything over an hour until temperatures break. And if sleep stays under 6 hr for another week, tell me in the next check-in and we will trim the long run rather than force it.

safetyCallouts.title: Sleep and heat are stacking.
safetyCallouts.body: Five and a half hours a night with a broken AC is a recovery problem, not just a comfort one. If sleep stays under 6 hr once the AC is back, or you feel dizzy, unusually breathless or get chest symptoms on a run, stop and see a doctor rather than push through.
